AI removed the engineering bottleneck across my 25 portfolio companies.  
I expected growth to follow.  
But it increasingly seems like the fastest shippers are the slowest growers.

For years, every founder I backed said the same thing:
"We'd grow faster if we could just ship faster."

Then AI removed the engineering constraint across roughly 25 companies in my portfolio.

And growth isn't necessarily what followed.
What followed in most cases was feature creep.

The companies shipping the fastest became the companies whose adoption lagged the most.

Shipping velocity and customer adoption are decoupling and most founders haven't turned the corner to realize that just yet

One portfolio company has a CTO who ships like crazy.
AI-assisted development, rapid releases, features deployed rapidly.

But customer adoption is lagging.
The same customer who begged for a fix yesterday is now afraid of the next release.

There was too much to use, too much to learn, and too much change to absorb all at once.

If shipping more starts to make your customers anxious, then you have a demand bottleneck.

Look at open source right now.

AI-assisted pull requests are increasing rapidly across every major project.
The cost of producing code collapsed but the cost of reviewing,
integrating, and absorbing it didn't move at all.

The bottleneck relocated downstream.

-  In open source, the bottleneck shifted to code review
-  In product companies, it moved to customer adoption
- In revenue terms, it landed squarely on demand

More software that doesn't necessarily drive revenue but it certainly incurs more cost and more things that have to be adopted  by your end user.

This will be the predictable result of removing engineering constraints without a demand constraint that replaces it.
AI made code cheap and cheap code revealed that customers R always paying for outcomes, clarity, and adoption.

3 weeks in the coding cave.

After a huuuge Product Hunt launch, some people probably expected us to celebrate, do interviews and enjoy the moment.

Instead, we disappeared. Why?

Because we shipped too early.

Which, to be fair, was exactly the plan.
We wanted to get Unabyss into people's hands as quickly as possible, learn from real usage, and see if the problem we were solving was actually worth solving.

The response was amazing.
People loved the idea. They loved the direction.

But they were also brutally honest.
Some features weren't optimized. Some integrations failed. There were rough edges everywhere.

And honestly, that's exactly what happens when something leaves the safety of internal testing and starts dealing with real workflows.

Here's the important part.
Despite all the issues, we got a very clear signal: this is what people want.
Not something adjacent.

Not a nice-to-have.

Something they've actively been looking for and are willing to pay for.
So we took all the feedback, locked ourselves away for three weeks and got back to work.

Today we're releasing Unabyss-1.1 [codename: Karamba].

A lot of fixes. A lot of improvements. A lot of lessons implemented.
And if you want the fastest way to understand what Unabyss is supposed to be, just connect it to Claude through MCP.
It'll take care of the rest.
And the rest is where things start getting interesting.

The AI labs will not own the enterprise use case layer. Not a technology problem. A positioning one.

"Why would I not build it with Claude?” The labs ship extraordinary models. But none of that lets them own the work that runs in production.

Why?

No serious buyer accepts 1 vendor owning the model, the copilots, and every use case on top. 

3 layers of lock-in stacked on each other. The worst possible seat at the table for a buyer.

So a layer has to sit between the model and the solution.

Its job: keep your use cases LLM-agnostic. Route frontier models where they earn their cost, smaller and open-source models where they don't, and swap any of them as the market moves, without re-architecting the workflow underneath.

We've seen this before. 
Hyperscalers had the best infrastructure, the deepest talent, and effectively unlimited capital. They still never owned the use cases that ran on top of them. 
The outcomes accrued to whoever built across clouds, not inside one.

Great technology at the platform layer has never translated into owning the outcome layer.

The labs sell models. Someone still has to deliver the outcome. Reliably, across every system the work touches, on infrastructure the enterprise controls.

That work is LLM-agnostic by design. Which is exactly why it won't belong to the labs.

I lead a team that builds agentic AI systems, and I'm not a developer myself. Most of what we produce is something I trust rather than read line by line.

The first part of this is familiar by now: AI tooling lets one person produce what used to take a team, and that creates real verification and complexity problems. True, and well covered. The part I think we're underrating is what all this speed does to the value of an aligned team member.

When output was slow, someone who didn't fully understand what mattered to the company, or didn't much care, could only do so much. The work itself was the rate limiter. That limiter is gone. Now the gap between what a person is building and what the company actually needs gets expressed at full speed and full volume. Misunderstanding scales. Indifference scales.

That makes two ordinary-sounding company capabilities worth far more than they were a few years ago.

- The first is clarity. Every person on the team should be able to tell the difference between impressive and valuable without you in the room. Most companies think they've done this and haven't. They've shared the strategy deck. They have not made it so clear what advances the business that an excited engineer at 11pm, with no one watching, knows which side of that line they're on. That is a much higher bar, and it is now the bar.

- The second is motivation, the real kind. Whether your people actually give a damn about where the company goes. This matters across the whole spectrum. Someone optimizing for their own title can now generate waste faster than ever, and in the worst case real damage, like a vulnerability that ships before anyone catches it. 

But the person I think about more is your best engineer. Genuinely excited, enormously productive, and not necessarily asking whether what they're building serves the business, because nothing in their world is making them ask. No bad actor anywhere. The enthusiasm just isn't pointed, and at this velocity, unpointed enthusiasm is expensive.

You should still build the machinery. Tooling, process, a human whose job is to pressure-test what gets built. But machinery is a backstop. It catches the wrong work after it exists. Clarity and motivation are what keep the wrong work from getting built with full conviction in the first place.

Here is where I land. When one person's output can outrun everyone's ability to check it, "I have good people" stops being enough on its own. What matters now is whether those good people understand what good means here, and whether they want it as badly as you do.

For a while now I've been building something I call ARB — a system that lets me run several AI coding agents at once and, more importantly, doesn't let them lie to me about whether the work is actually done.

That second part is the whole point.

Most multi-agent setups are good at coordination — routing work between models, running them in parallel, stitching the results together. The part almost nobody handles is trust: how do you know the output is correct, and not just plausible? Agents are very good at producing work that looks finished. A test that passes because it checks the wrong thing. A fix that satisfies the prompt but not the actual problem. A confident "done" with nothing real behind it.

ARB is built around a single rule: nothing is trusted, everything is verified. Different models from different labs review each other's work, because models from the same family share blind spots. Verification has to be earned by a hard signal — a test that genuinely fails before the fix and passes after — not asserted. And the checks are designed so they can't be quietly satisfied by a shortcut, because the most dangerous failure isn't an agent that gets it wrong, it's an agent that gets it wrong and tells you it got it right.

I've been running it to build and ship real production software — multiple products, solo, in parallel — and the discipline is the reason the speed doesn't turn into slop.

I'm going to write up some of what I've learned building it, because the lessons are more interesting than the architecture: the specific ways these systems fool themselves, and the patterns for catching it. The first one's coming soon.
If you're building with agents and have hit the "it said it was done but it wasn't" wall — that wall is the whole problem, and it's a solvable one.

One trend I don't see discussed enough:
As AI models improve, search quality becomes even more important.
Most people assume better models automatically produce better answers.
In reality, answer quality is increasingly limited by retrieval quality.
A model can only reason effectively with the information it receives.
If your search system surfaces outdated, incomplete, or irrelevant information, even the most advanced model will struggle.
This is why I believe the next generation of AI products won't compete solely on model performance.
They'll compete on:
• Information retrieval
• Data freshness
• Ranking quality
• Context construction
• Knowledge organization
The future of AI is not just about generating answers.
It's about finding the right information before generation begins.
Retrieval is becoming the new moat.

⚠️ More AI-generated code can quietly make your team slower. Here's the mechanism nobody puts on the roadmap.

A model generates in an hour more than a person can carefully read in a day. Every line it produces is still a line someone has to read, review, and own, drawing on the same scarce attention the bottleneck was always about.

So volume without understanding isn't progress. It's debt with a shorter fuse.

The trap is subtle. Twenty-five years ago, Joel Spolsky noticed that programmers prefer writing to reading, because writing feels like progress. With AI, that preference turns dangerous. The accelerator becomes a dependency, until the only thing that truly understands your system is the machine that wrote it.

And the dangerous output is never the code that fails to compile. That's easy to catch. It's the code that compiles, runs, survives a quick glance, and is quietly wrong. Fluency is not truth.

The engineers who can tell those apart don't get automated away. They become the people the whole team routes its decisions through. That's not a smaller role. It's a bigger one.

I've put the full argument, including why some of these limits are mathematical and won't be patched away, into a paper. It lands in a few days.

For now: where have you watched "looks right" quietly turn into "was wrong"?

Networking is the slowest way to grow a network.

Here's a 10x faster way (I did it twice this year):

The first story:

Three weeks ago I open sourced Newsjack.sh, 20 AI skills that turn Claude into a PR team. 

In 14 days, it's opened more doors than 18 months of networking combined. 

Founders, executives, journalists, 20-year operators, agency owners. People that I'd never have gotten a reply from are now showing up in my DM.

All of a sudden my calendar was full for 2 weeks straight and I'm pulled in 15 directions.

I'm completely overwhelmed. Honestly? In a good way.

Then here's story #2:

Back in February I published an essay on how I run my AI agent team to ship software faster than a team of 10 developers. 

It hit 5 million views on X. My account grew from 6k to 26k overnight. 

Hundreds of investors showed up in my follower list, including partners at YC, a16z, and Sequoia, plus a handful of people whose YouTube channels and courses I used to binge for hours and hours. People I quietly admired from a distance now show up in my orbit.

So that's my stories.

Two pieces of work. Two completely different audiences. Same dynamic.

And here's the real lesson:

Putting yourself out there is asymmetric.

The downside is a post flops and maybe someone you don't talk to anymore have a chuckle. 

The upside is a Sequoia partner in your DMs, or a customer you didn't know existed, or a hero of yours quote-tweeting your work. You can't get that ratio anywhere else. Not from a networking event.

If you're growing a business or a career, here's what I'd actually optimize for:

Make something useful and put it out there. For free. 

A tool. A piece of writing. A open-source repo. A case study. A video. 

Anything that is so good that it makes people question why you do it.

Networking gives you linear returns. You trade your time for someone else's, and the most valuable people you want to meet won't make that trade.

Putting yourself in the public gives you compounding returns. One piece of work can keep introducing you for years.

Stop optimizing for the room.

Optimize for the work.

In case you didn't know – that is the reality we're living in now (and probably will for the foreseeable future.) After Fable, it's now the GPT-5.6 release that got stopped by government decision. Let's face it: The best AI models in the world are developed by a small group of people, and now another small group of people decides who gets to use them. 

I'm not surprised by this. 

Did anyone really think that when a country found AGI, they would happily give it to everyone else? 

Sovereign AI is no longer a theoretical concept but a harsh reality that we (especially everyone outside the US and China) have to face NOW.

In practical terms, this means that whatever business workflow you're building on top of AI right now, you should keep models interchangeable and work with the LLMs that we have right now – not anticipate that the process will "get better" once you get better models. 

Maybe you never will.

I call this principle the Freeze Test and wrote about it almost exactly one year ago.
